text:
Anya: Quick sync on cache invalidation patterns for console queries + RBAC. Wanted to capture options and ops tradeoffs.
Ravi: go for it.
Anya: problem: when a permission changes we either need to evict a whole set of cached responses or apply filtering at read time. Both have costs.
Becca: TL;DR: evict = simpler correctness, filter = more CPU/latency.
Tom: also consider burst invalidation storms if an admin rolls many policies at once.
Ravi: true — we saw that in staging when a script updated 2k users. Cache thrash.
Anya: options we sketched: 1) TTL-heavy: short TTL for tenant-keyed entries; 2) event-driven invalidation: subscribe to policy changes and evict precisely; 3) versioned keys: include policy_hash in cache key; 4) hybrid tiering: coarse-grain tiered keys + final filter.
Becca: TTL-heavy reduces invalidation complexity but increases miss rate and upstream load. Not great for bursty dashboards.
Tom: event-driven sounds ideal, but delivery guarantees matter. If we miss a change -> leakage of stale perms.
Ravi: we can tolerate short windows of staleness for non-sensitive panels, but not for admin flows. Need route-level sensitivity.
Anya: agreed. We should classify routes by sensitivity: strict (no staleness), soft (few seconds ok), relaxed (minutes okay).
Becca: versioned keys (include policy_rev id) are attractive: when policy changes, rev increments -> old keys naturally expire. But key cardinality skyrockets with many tenants.
Tom: cardinality + storage blowup. Need evictions + compaction.
Ravi: what about optimistic invalidation with backoff? On policy change we mark a tombstone key and gradually evict tenant partitions to avoid thundering herd.
Anya: tombstone + staggered background sweeps could work. We can also add rate limits on evictions per node.
Becca: to reduce cardinality, we could bucket tenants by permission cohort (e.g., company-tier) and only use cohort keys for most traffic, fallback to per-tenant check for exceptions. Similar to tiered cache idea but cohort driven.
Tom: cohorting needs good telemetry to detect outliers.
Ravi: continuous-batching implications: if we add per-tenant filtering at the edge, batch coalescing decreases. We've measured up to 25% less effective batching when responses are unique by tenant.
Anya: we could separate batching domain: batch at model/prefix layer before auth; then apply lightweight per-tenant filter. That preserves some coalescing.
Becca: but if filters are heavy (complex policy predicates) we lose net benefit.
Tom: streaming panels (live preview) care a lot about p95. For those routes, prefer control-plane evaluation + small TTL.
Anya: agreed. Route-level policy: streaming -> control plane quickpath; analytics tiles -> cohorted cache + eventual filter.
Ravi: infra note: policy service already emits events on policy change to kafka topic "policy.changes" with payload {tenant,policy_rev,hash}. We can wire cache invalidator.
infra-bot: policy service: emitted event schema v1 at 2024-09-12T10:02:00Z. Consumer group recommended: console-cache-invalidator.
Anya: good — event-driven invalidation plan now looks feasible if we add delivery ack and periodic reconciliation job to guard against misses.
Becca: reconciliation job (full scan) should run in low-traffic windows and be rate-limited.
Ravi: ops question: how do we avoid eviction-induced traffic spike?
Anya: strategies: stagger evictions, pre-warm by proactively recomputing top-N keys for affected tenants, and use per-node eviction quotas.
Tom: pre-warm is nice but expensive. Maybe pre-warm only if active dashboards > threshold.
Becca: instrumentation: track metrics: invalidation.count, invalidation.duration, cache.hit_rate_by_route, evicted_keys_per_min, prewarm_failures.
Ravi: and batch-coalesce-rate to ensure we don't regress serving efficiency.
Anya: config sketch:
```
console.auth_policy.mode: event|ttl|versioned|hybrid
console.cache.cohort_size: 128
console.eviction.stagger_ms: 200
console.eviction.max_per_node_per_min: 500
console.reconcile.cron: "0 3 * * *"
feature_flag.console_rbac_v2: off
```
Ravi: rollout: start in hybrid mode for 10% orgs with event invalidations + tombstone + reconcile enabled. Monitor metrics for 48h.
Becca: add canary triggers: spike in evicted_keys_per_min or drop in batch-coalesce-rate -> auto-disable event invalidation.
Tom: for debugging, capture policy_rev header on responses: X-Policy-Rev: <rev>. Also log cache_key and cohort_id for top 1% misses.
Anya: I'll add those headers.
Ravi: edge case: what if a policy change reopens access (grant) — should we proactively rebuild caches or let them warm? Rebuilding helps UX for newly granted users.
Becca: maybe rebuild for grants if tenant activity > threshold; otherwise let it lazy-warm.
Tom: need ACL to prevent scripts from mass-granting to accidentally induce pre-warm costs.
Anya: ops playbook: 1) disable event invalidation (ff) 2) enable ttl-only fallback 3) run reconcile 4) re-enable canary. I'll sketch in runbook.
Ravi: I'll wire the kafka consumer and reconciliation job. Becca: I'll add telemetry and headers. Tom: I'll update serving docs with route-level policy mapping.
Anya: final decision? do hybrid: cohort keys + event invalidation + reconcile + route exceptions for streaming?
All: +1
Anya: thanks all. I'll file the follow-up RFC with experiment checklist and assign tasks.
Ravi: I'll post the consumer PR.
Becca: will add metrics dashboards.
Tom: will draft the runbook.
infra-bot: reminder: schedule canary ramp with feature-flag service and include alert: console.cache.eviction.rate > 1000/min.
Anya: closing. I'll ping when RFC is up.
